title: Tuning Charge Density Wave transitions through lattice strain in NbSe3
authors: Antoine Gallo Frantz, Aleksander Sinchenko, Luc Ortega, Pavel Grigoriev, Vladislav Kochev, Pierre Godard, Pierre Olivier Renault, Dominique Thiaudiere, David Le Bolloch, Vincent Jacques
abstract: The Charge Density Wave (CDW) state is a perfect example of a combined structural and electronic state, both characterized by a periodic lattice distortion and an electronic modulation of condensed electrons, resulting from electron-phonon coupling. They are thus prone to be tuned by lattice strain. NbSe3 is a prototypical example of CDW states, with a chain-like structure displaying two CDWs at 145K and 59K, with wavevectors along and inclined with respect to the chain axis b. Here, we report on the evolution of the lattice structure and CDW properties in the quasi-one-dimensional charge-density-wave system NbSe3 under tensile stresses applied along and perpendicular to the chains axis b by a combination of X-ray diffraction and transport measurements. We find that the lattice structure show exotic Poissons coefficients and strongly anisotropic Youngs moduli while the evolution of the electrical resistance demonstrates shifts of both charge-density-wave critical temperatures that are strongly correlated with the lattice parameters. The two CDW transitions display different behaviours under applied stresses, and suggest that a modification of the band curvature leads to the observed transport signatures.
summary: This work experimentally demonstrates that applying uniaxial lattice strain to NbSe3 significantly tunes its two distinct Charge Density Wave (CDW) transitions. By combining X-ray diffraction with transport measurements, the authors establish a quantitative, linear correlation between the material's structural parameters and the critical temperatures of the CDW states. This highlights the extreme sensitivity of correlated electronic phases to mechanical boundary conditions.
main_problem: The study investigates how applying mechanical lattice strain (tensile stress) tunes the Charge Density Wave (CDW) transitions in the quasi-one-dimensional material NbSe3.
main_result: The CDW critical temperatures ($T_{c1}, T_{c2}$) show strong, predictable linear correlations with the applied strain and resulting lattice parameters, suggesting the CDW state is highly sensitive to lattice geometry.
method: The research combines *in-situ* X-ray diffraction (XRD) to measure lattice strain and elastic constants with transport measurements to track the temperature-dependent electrical resistance anomalies associated with the CDW transitions.
model_or_system: The system is NbSe3, a prototypical quasi-1D conductor known for exhibiting multiple CDW states. The analysis models the coupling between structural distortions (lattice strain) and electronic instabilities (CDW formation) using elastic theory and electronic susceptibility calculations.
key_observables: CDW critical temperatures ($T_{c1}=145	ext{ K}, T_{c2}=59	ext{ K}$), electrical resistance changes ($\alpha_1, \alpha_2$), lattice parameters ($a, b, c, \alpha,  eta, \gamma$), and elastic constants (Young's moduli, Poisson's coefficients).
important_parameters: Applied uniaxial tensile stresses ($\sigma_b, \sigma_c$), lattice strain ($\epsilon$), and the ratio of lattice parameters ($c/a$, $1/b$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the linear elastic regime for strain calculations and that the changes in conductivity are dominated by modifications to the band curvature rather than just the superconducting gap magnitude.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of the six lattice parameters versus applied forces, and show the temperature dependence of resistance curves under varying tensile stresses, mapping out the shifts in $T_c$ and resistance jumps.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents mechanical characterization (XRD/elastic constants) followed by electronic characterization (transport measurements), establishing a quantitative link between the measured structural changes and the resulting shifts in the CDW transition temperatures and associated transport signatures.
why_interesting: The strong coupling between mechanical strain and electronic phase transitions (CDW) is a key area of condensed matter physics. Understanding how external mechanical fields can tune correlated electronic states provides insights applicable to designing novel electronic materials.
